◇ Note. The hardened heart problem. Sihon’s refusal to allow Israelite passage is attributed directly to Yahweh’s hardening of his spirit — the same theological language used of Pharaoh in Exod 4:21, 7:3, 9:12, etc. The pattern raises the OT’s most persistent moral-theological tension: divine sovereignty over human refusal that nonetheless remains accountable as refusal. The Pharaoh narratives carefully alternate "Pharaoh hardened his heart" and "Yahweh hardened Pharaoh’s heart" formulas; here Deuteronomy collapses the distinction toward the divine causation. Paul’s extended discussion in Rom 9:14–24 (citing Exod 9:16 directly) is the NT’s most sustained engagement with this theological problem. Augustine, Calvin, and Aquinas read the passages differently — but the textual phenomenon Paul is grappling with begins at verses like this one, where divine causation and human responsibility are affirmed simultaneously without the OT showing any felt need to systematize the apparent tension.

◇ Note. The Israelite court system. The verse institutes a tribal judicial structure — judges (shofetim) and officers (shoterim, likely court-marshals or enforcement officers) at every city gate. The "gate" was the OT’s standard public legal venue (Ruth 4:1–11, Boaz’s court case; Amos 5:10, "they hate him who reproves in the gate"; Job 29:7, the patriarch’s public seat at the gate). Archaeological work at Iron Age Israelite city-gates (Tel Dan, Beersheba, Gezer) has revealed bench-lined gate-chambers consistent with this judicial-administrative function. The chapter’s next verses (16:19–20) prohibit bribery and partiality and famously command "Justice, justice (tzedek tzedek) you shall pursue" — the doubled noun is one of the OT’s most cited rhetorical intensifiers. The verse establishes the institutional framework for Israelite local justice that operates throughout the monarchic period.

◇ Note. The parapet law. The verse is the OT’s clearest articulation of negligence liability: the householder must build a parapet on the flat roof (the standard Levantine roof-form, used as living and sleeping space) to prevent falls. The principle — that the builder bears responsibility for foreseeable harm — anticipates modern tort doctrines of duty of care, premises liability, and the general principle that creating a foreseeable risk imposes obligations to mitigate it. Rabbinic tradition (b. Bava Kamma 15b) generalizes the verse into the requirement to remove any dangerous condition from one’s property — a swimming pool, a vicious dog, a damaged ladder — and treats it as the textual root of Jewish negligence law. The verse is one of the OT’s most institutionally durable texts, with descendants in nearly every developed legal tradition.

◇ Note. The interest prohibition. The verse forbids lending at interest to a fellow Israelite (cf. Exod 22:25, Lev 25:35–37) while permitting it to foreigners (23:20). The asymmetry encodes a specifically covenantal economic ethic: financial gain from a brother’s misfortune is prohibited, but participation in the wider commercial credit economy is permitted. The verse becomes the textual ground for Christian and Jewish anti-usury traditions (medieval canon law, the rabbinic halakhic debates over ribbit, the Church’s Lateran prohibitions) and indirectly for the historical limitation of Jewish economic life to lending professions in medieval Europe (Christians forbidding usury internally created the niche). Modern Islamic finance (the prohibition of riba) descends from the same tradition. The verse is one of the OT’s most economically consequential texts, generating two and a half millennia of legal-religious adaptation.

◇ Note. The first-fruits confession. The chapter prescribes a liturgical recitation accompanying the offering of first-fruits — the so-called "Wandering Aramean" creed (26:5–10) — and verse 8 is the credal core. The text is the OT’s clearest example of a fixed liturgical confession: Israel must say specific words ("a wandering Aramean was my father…"), not just bring the offering. Most OT scholarship since Gerhard von Rad’s "The Form-Critical Problem of the Hexateuch" (1938) treats this confession as one of the oldest credal kernels of Israelite faith — possibly preserving pre-monarchic liturgical tradition. The phrase "with a mighty hand and an outstretched arm" recurs across the Pentateuch (Exod 6:6, Deut 4:34, 5:15, 26:8, Ps 136:12) as Israel’s standard exodus-formula, and it enters the Passover Haggadah essentially verbatim. The verse is the textual root of Jewish liturgical historical confession that descends through the Haggadah to modern Passover practice.

◇ Note. The Levites’ liturgical curses. The chapter stages a covenant-renewal ceremony on entering the land: half the tribes on Mount Gerizim recite the blessings, half on Mount Ebal recite the curses, with the Levites pronouncing twelve specific anathemas (27:15–26) to which the people respond "Amen." The format is theologically precise — covenants in the ANE typically included blessings and curses (Hittite vassal treaties, the Sefire inscriptions); the OT’s innovation is the antiphonal liturgical staging with named geography. The twelve curses cover idolatry (27:15), parental dishonor (16), social-economic abuse of the vulnerable (17–19), forbidden sexual relations (20–23), homicide and judicial bribery (24–25), and a comprehensive closing curse (26, "cursed is he who does not confirm the words of this law to do them" — the verse Paul will weaponize in Gal 3:10). The chapter is one of the OT’s clearest demonstrations that covenant is liturgical event, not just text.

◇ Note. The rhetorical-monolatrous question. Moses’ prayer poses the question — what god in heaven or earth can do such works as Yahweh? — in a form that does not categorically deny other gods’ existence but asserts Yahweh’s incomparable power among them. The construction is characteristic of Israelite monolatrous theology in its earlier strata: the existence of the surrounding pantheon is acknowledged or left untouched, while Yahweh’s practical supremacy is asserted (compare Exod 15:11, "Who is like you, Yahweh, among the gods?"; Ps 86:8, 89:6). The fully developed monotheistic claim — that other gods do not exist at all — emerges most clearly in Second Isaiah (Isa 44:6, 45:5–6, 18). The verse is one of many that show the OT theological development from monolatry (one Yahweh among real gods) toward strict monotheism (Yahweh alone is real) as a long process internal to the canon, not a single moment.

◇ Note. The wilderness-rebellion catalog. The chapter rehearses Israel’s wilderness failures — the golden calf at Horeb (9:8–21), the rebellion at Taberah, Massah, Kibroth-hattaavah (9:22), and the refusal to enter the land at Kadesh-barnea (9:23). The rhetorical function is preventive: Moses recites the failures so that Israel cannot, on entering the land, mistake survival for moral worthiness. The same pattern of wilderness-rebellion recital recurs at Pss 78, 95, 106, and Ezek 20 — each generation re-tells the failures to prevent its own. The Christian Letter to the Hebrews (Heb 3:7–4:11) extends the pattern to the church: the wilderness rebellion is the warning case for any community in covenant relationship with Yahweh. The verse is a structural pillar of the OT’s wisdom-by-failure pedagogy, where Israel’s religious instruction proceeds primarily by remembered catastrophe rather than abstract precept.

◇ Ephrem the Syrian (365). Ephrem the Syrian Commentary on Deuteronomy (c. 365 AD)

On 'the place which the Lord your God shall choose out of all your tribes to put his name there' (Deu 12:5), Ephrem reads the centralization-of-worship command as the canonical Old-Testament typological anchor that flows through Shiloh → Jerusalem → Zion → the Eucharistic altar of every local church. The Lord chooses ONE place for his Name in the Old Covenant; in the New Covenant, every Eucharistic altar is THE chosen place because the Body broken there IS the New-Covenant tabot. Tewahedo eucharistic theology cites Deu 12:5 as the canonical anchor for the doctrine that the Eucharist gathers Jerusalem's centralization into every parish — the tabot-bearing altar IS the chosen place.

◇ Note. Profane slaughter. The verse marks one of Deuteronomy’s most consequential legal innovations: the desacralization of ordinary meat-eating. Earlier Pentateuchal law (Lev 17:3–4) treated all animal slaughter as cultic — every killing of an animal had to be brought to the sanctuary as a peace-offering, with the blood disposed of properly. Deuteronomy, anticipating cult centralization at one distant sanctuary, makes ordinary slaughter for food permitted "in all your gates" — within any town — provided the blood is poured out (12:16). The legal change is enormous: meat consumption is partially uncoupled from sacrifice, and a distinction between sacred and ordinary slaughter enters Israelite practice for the first time. Most scholars treat this provision as one of the strongest internal indicators that Deuteronomy was composed (or radically edited) during the seventh-century push toward Jerusalem-centric worship, when the practical impossibility of bringing every animal to one sanctuary required a legal accommodation. The verse quietly transforms how Israelites actually ate.

◇ Ephrem the Syrian (365). Ephrem the Syrian Commentary on Deuteronomy (c. 365 AD)

On the king's Torah — 'when he sitteth upon the throne of his kingdom, he shall write him a copy of this law in a book' (Deu 17:18-19) — Ephrem reads the king-as-Torah-scribe command as the canonical Old-Testament anchor of the doctrine that the king is FIRST a guardian of the law, only secondarily a ruler of the people. The king does not stand above the Torah; he copies it with his own hand and reads it all the days of his life. Tewahedo Solomonic-dynasty self-understanding, codified in the Kǝbrä Nägäśt (Glory of the Kings), cites Deu 17:18 as the canonical Old-Testament warrant for the Ethiopian-emperor-as-Torah-guardian — the emperor at coronation receives both crown and Tabot, and is sworn to defend both.

epub:type="footnote">

◇ Ephrem the Syrian (365). Ephrem the Syrian Commentary on Deuteronomy (c. 365 AD)

On 'Cursed be he that confirmeth not all the words of this law to do them' (Deu 27:26), Ephrem reads the final Ebal-curse as the canonical Old-Testament anchor of Paul's argument in Galatians 3:10 ('as many as are of the works of the law are under the curse: for it is written, Cursed is every one that continueth not in all things which are written in the book of the law to do them' — verbatim citation). The total-law requirement makes salvation-by-works impossible: no one keeps all things. The verse becomes the typological seed of the apostolic gospel of grace. Tewahedo soteriology cites Deu 27:26 + Gal 3:10 as the canonical doubled-witness that the law diagnoses the curse the Cross removes.

⌘ Hebrew. Am s’gullah (עַם סְגֻלָּה). "A treasured people" — the term s’gullah means a personal treasure, the kind a king might keep separately from the public treasury. The same term describes Israel in Exod 19:5, Deut 7:6, 26:18, and Mal 3:17 (where the righteous are Yahweh’s s’gullah "in the day that I make"). The Christian appropriation of the term — 1 Pet 2:9, "a people for his own possession" — applies the formula to the Church, with conscious dependence on the Septuagint Greek (laos eis peripoiēsin). The verse encodes Israel’s self-understanding as the deity’s personal portion among the nations — a status that is theologically positive (covenant election) and practically demanding (the dietary and ritual distinctiveness the chapter goes on to detail). The chosen-people theology has had a long and complicated history; the OT itself uses the term for both blessing and obligation simultaneously.

◇ Note. The Zelophehad daughters return. The chapter reopens the question first decided in Num 27 (where Zelophehad’s daughters won the right to inherit their father’s portion). The Manassite elders raise a complication: if the daughters marry outside the tribe, the inheritance leaves Manasseh permanently. The resolution: they may marry whomever they please — but only within the tribe of Manasseh. The chapter is the OT’s clearest case of a single inheritance-law working through successive cases over multiple chapters, with each iteration refining the principle: women may inherit (ch 27), women must marry within their tribe to preserve tribal patrimony (ch 36). The narrative arc — five named daughters as protagonists across two chapters of legal innovation — is one of the OT’s most extended treatments of female legal agency, even within the constraints the second ruling reimposes. Rabbinic tradition (b. Bava Batra 119b) celebrates the daughters as one of the great legal-precedent cases of Israelite jurisprudence.

⌘ Hebrew. ʼădônây (אֲדֹנָי). the Lord (used as a proper name of God only). [Reviewer: extend this with context, theological reading, and any cross-canon resonance before promoting.]

◇ Note. The general principle. The chapter generalizes the Zelophehad-daughter case into universal principle: any daughter who inherits in any tribe must marry within that tribe to preserve tribal land. The provision encodes Israel’s fundamental principle of tribal land-inalienability: nakhalah (inheritance) is not just real estate but the visible embodiment of tribal-covenantal identity, and its movement across tribal boundaries is treated as a category-violation. The same principle drives the Levitical Jubilee laws (Lev 25:23–28) where land returns to original families every fiftieth year, and the prophetic outrage at Naboth’s vineyard (1 Kgs 21) — Ahab’s offer to buy is precisely the violation Naboth refuses ("I will not give you the inheritance of my fathers"). The chapter closes the book of Numbers with a small case-law resolution that nonetheless encodes one of the most distinctive features of Israelite social-religious thought: land as sacred trust rather than commodity. The principle has had a long afterlife in Catholic social teaching and modern theologies of land justice.

There you will offer yourselves to your enemies for male and female slaves, and nobody will buy you. Numbers 36:1“The heads of the fathers’ households of the family of the children of Gilead, the son of Machir, the son of Manasseh, of the families of the sons of Joseph, came near and spoke before Moses and before the princes, the heads of the fathers’ households of the children of Israel.” Hebrew (Masoretic / WLC) וַֽיִּקְרְב֞וּ רָאשֵׁ֣י הָֽאָב֗וֹת לְמִשְׁפַּ֤חַת בְּנֵֽי־גִלְעָד֙ בֶּן־מָכִ֣יר בֶּן־מְנַשֶּׁ֔ה מִֽמִּשְׁפְּחֹ֖ת בְּנֵ֣י יוֹסֵ֑ף וַֽיְדַבְּר֞וּ לִפְנֵ֤י מֹשֶׁה֙ וְלִפְנֵ֣י הַנְּשִׂאִ֔ים רָאשֵׁ֥י אָב֖וֹת לִבְנֵ֥י יִשְׂרָאֵֽל׃ Greek (Septuagint / Brenton) Καὶ προσῆλθον οἱ ἄρχοντες φυλῆς υἱῶν Γαλαὰδ υἱοῦ Μαχὶρ υἱοῦ Μανασσῆ ἐκ τῆς φυλῆς υἱῶν Ἰωσὴφ, καὶ ἐλάλησαν ἔναντι Μωυσῆ, καὶ ἔναντι Ἐλεάζαρ τοῦ ἱερέως, καὶ ἔναντι τῶν ἀρχόντων οἴκων πατριῶν τῶν υἱῶν Ἰσραὴλ, ↩ Numbers 36:2“They said, “Yahweh commanded my lord to give the land for inheritance by lot to the children of Israel. My lord was commanded by Yahweh to give the inheritance of Zelophehad our brother to his daughters.” Hebrew (Masoretic / WLC) וַיֹּאמְר֗וּ אֶת־אֲדֹנִי֙ צִוָּ֣ה יְהוָ֔ה לָתֵ֨ת אֶת־הָאָ֧רֶץ בְּנַחֲלָ֛ה בְּגוֹרָ֖ל לִבְנֵ֣י יִשְׂרָאֵ֑ל וַֽאדֹנִי֙ צֻוָּ֣ה בַֽיהוָ֔ה לָתֵ֗ת אֶֽת־נַחֲלַ֛ת צְלָפְחָ֥ד אָחִ֖ינוּ לִבְנֹתָֽיו׃ Greek (Septuagint / Brenton) καὶ εἶπαν, τῷ κυρῖῳ ἡμῶν ἐνετείλατο Κύριος ἀποδοῦναι τὴν γῆν τῆς κληρονομίας ἐν κλήρῳ τοῖς υἱοῖς Ἰσραήλ· καὶ τῷ κυρίῳ συνέταξε Κύριος δοῦναι τὴν κληρονομίαν Σαλπαὰδ τοῦ ἀδελφοῦ ἡμῶν ταῖς θυγατράσιν αὐτοῦ. ↩ Numbers 36:3“If they are married to any of the sons of the other tribes of the children of Israel, then their inheritance will be taken away from the inheritance of our fathers, and will be added to the inheritance of the tribe to which they shall belong. So it will be taken away from the lot of our inheritance.” Hebrew (Masoretic / WLC) וְ֠הָיוּ לְאֶחָ֞ד מִבְּנֵ֨י שִׁבְטֵ֥י בְנֵֽי־יִשְׂרָאֵל֮ לְנָשִׁים֒ וְנִגְרְעָ֤ה נַחֲלָתָן֙ מִנַּחֲלַ֣ת אֲבֹתֵ֔ינוּ וְנוֹסַ֕ף עַ֚ל נַחֲלַ֣ת הַמַּטֶּ֔ה אֲשֶׁ֥ר תִּהְיֶ֖ינָה לָהֶ֑ם וּמִגֹּרַ֥ל נַחֲלָתֵ֖נוּ יִגָּרֵֽעַ׃ Greek (Septuagint / Brenton) Καὶ ἔσονται ἑνὶ τῶν φυλῶν υἱῶν Ἰσραὴλ γυναῖκες· καὶ ἀφαιρεθήσεται ὁ κλῆρος αὐτῶν ἐκ τῆς κατασχέσεως τῶν πατέρεν ἡμῶν, καὶ προστεθήσεται εἰς κληρονομίαν τῆς φυλῆς, οἷς ἂν γένωνται γυναῖκες, καὶ ἐκ τοῦ κλήρου τῆς κληρονομίας ἡμῶν ἀφαιρεθήσεται. ↩ Numbers 36:4“When the jubilee of the children of Israel comes, then their inheritance will be added to the inheritance of the tribe to which they shall belong. So their inheritance will be taken away from the inheritance of the tribe of our fathers.”” Hebrew (Masoretic / WLC) וְאִם־יִהְיֶ֣ה הַיֹּבֵל֮ לִבְנֵ֣י יִשְׂרָאֵל֒ וְנֽוֹסְפָה֙ נַחֲלָתָ֔ן עַ֚ל נַחֲלַ֣ת הַמַּטֶּ֔ה אֲשֶׁ֥ר תִּהְיֶ֖ינָה לָהֶ֑ם וּמִֽנַּחֲלַת֙ מַטֵּ֣ה אֲבֹתֵ֔ינוּ יִגָּרַ֖ע נַחֲלָתָֽן׃ Greek (Septuagint / Brenton) Ἐὰν δὲ γένηται ἡ ἄφεσις τῶν υἱῶν Ἰσραὴλ, καὶ προστεθήσεται ἡ κληρονομία αὐτῶν ἐπὶ τὴν κληρονομίαν τῆς φυλῆς, οἷς ἂν γένωνται γυναῖκες, καὶ ἀπὸ τῆς κληρονομίας φυλῆς πατριᾶς ἡμῶν ἀφαιρεθήσεται ἡ κληρονομία αὐτῶν. ↩ Numbers 36:5“Moses commanded the children of Israel according to Yahweh’s word, saying, “The tribe of the sons of Joseph speak what is right.” Hebrew (Masoretic / WLC) וַיְצַ֤ו מֹשֶׁה֙ אֶת־בְּנֵ֣י יִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל עַל־פִּ֥י יְהוָ֖ה לֵאמֹ֑ר כֵּ֛ן מַטֵּ֥ה בְנֵֽי־יוֹסֵ֖ף דֹּבְרִֽים׃ Greek (Septuagint / Brenton) Καὶ ἐνετείλατο Μωυσῆς τοῖς υἱοῖς Ἰσραὴλ διὰ προστάγματος Κυρίου, λέγων, οὕτως φυλὴ υἱῶν Ἰωσὴφ λέγουσι. ↩ Numbers 36:6“This is the thing which Yahweh commands concerning the daughters of Zelophehad, saying, ‘Let them be married to whom they think best, only they shall marry into the family of the tribe of their father.” Hebrew (Masoretic / WLC) זֶ֣ה הַדָּבָ֞ר אֲשֶׁר־צִוָּ֣ה יְהוָ֗ה לִבְנ֤וֹת צְלָפְחָד֙ לֵאמֹ֔ר לַטּ֥וֹב בְּעֵינֵיהֶ֖ם תִּהְיֶ֣ינָה לְנָשִׁ֑ים אַ֗ךְ לְמִשְׁפַּ֛חַת מַטֵּ֥ה אֲבִיהֶ֖ם תִּהְיֶ֥ינָה לְנָשִֽׁים׃ Greek (Septuagint / Brenton) Τοῦτο τὸ ῥῆμα ὃ συνέταξε Κύριος ταῖς θυγατράσι Σαλπαὰδ, λέγων, οὗ ἀρέσκῃ ἐναντίον αὐτῶν, ἔστωσαν γυναῖκες, πλὴν ἐκ τοῦ δήμου τοῦ πατρὸς αὐτῶν ἔστωσαν γυναῖκες. ↩ Numbers 36:7“So shall no inheritance of the children of Israel move from tribe to tribe; for the children of Israel shall all keep the inheritance of the tribe of his fathers.” Hebrew (Masoretic / WLC) וְלֹֽא־תִסֹּ֤ב נַחֲלָה֙ לִבְנֵ֣י יִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל מִמַּטֶּ֖ה אֶל־מַטֶּ֑ה כִּ֣י אִ֗ישׁ בְּנַחֲלַת֙ מַטֵּ֣ה אֲבֹתָ֔יו יִדְבְּק֖וּ בְּנֵ֥י יִשְׂרָאֵֽל׃ Greek (Septuagint / Brenton) Καὶ οὐχὶ περιστραφήσεται κληρονομία τοῖς υἱοῖς Ἰσραὴλ ἀπὸ φυλῆς ἐπὶ φύλην, ὅτι ἕκαστος ἐν τῇ κληρονομίᾳ τῆς φυλῆς τῆς πατριᾶς αὐτοῦ προσκολληθήσονται οἱ υἱοὶ Ἰσραήλ. ↩ Numbers 36:8“Every daughter who possesses an inheritance in any tribe of the children of Israel shall be wife to one of the family of the tribe of her father, that the children of Israel may each possess the inheritance of his fathers.” Hebrew (Masoretic / WLC) וְכָל־בַּ֞ת יֹרֶ֣שֶׁת נַחֲלָ֗ה מִמַּטּוֹת֮ בְּנֵ֣י יִשְׂרָאֵל֒ לְאֶחָ֗ד מִמִּשְׁפַּ֛חַת מַטֵּ֥ה אָבִ֖יהָ תִּהְיֶ֣ה לְאִשָּׁ֑ה לְמַ֗עַן יִֽירְשׁוּ֙ בְּנֵ֣י יִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל אִ֖ישׁ נַחֲלַ֥ת אֲבֹתָֽיו׃ Greek (Septuagint / Brenton) Καὶ πᾶσα θυγάτηρ ἀγχιατεύουσα κληρονομίαν ἐκ τῶν φυλῶν υἱῶν Ἰσραὴλ, ἑνὶ τῶν ἐκ τοῦ δήμου τοῦ πατρὸς αὐτῆς ἔσονται γυναῖκες, ἵνα ἀγχιστεύσωσιν οἱ υἱοὶ Ἰσραὴλ ἕκαστος τὴν κληρονομίαν τὴν πατρικὴν αὐτοῦ. ↩ Numbers 36:9“So shall no inheritance move from one tribe to another tribe; for the tribes of the children of Israel shall each keep his own inheritance.’”” Hebrew (Masoretic / WLC) וְלֹֽא־תִסֹּ֧ב נַחֲלָ֛ה מִמַּטֶּ֖ה לְמַטֶּ֣ה אַחֵ֑ר כִּי־אִישׁ֙ בְּנַ֣חֲלָת֔וֹ יִדְבְּק֕וּ מַטּ֖וֹת בְּנֵ֥י יִשְׂרָאֵֽל׃ Greek (Septuagint / Brenton) Καὶ οὐ περιστραφήσεται ὁ κλῆρος ἐκ φυλῆς ἐπὶ φυλὴν ἑτέραν, ἀλλʼ ἕκαστος ἐν τῇ κληρονομίᾳ αὐτοῦ προσκολληθήσονται οἱ υἱοὶ Ἰσραήλ. ↩ Numbers 36:10“The daughters of Zelophehad did as Yahweh commanded Moses:” Hebrew (Masoretic / WLC) כַּאֲשֶׁ֛ר צִוָּ֥ה יְהוָ֖ה אֶת־מֹשֶׁ֑ה כֵּ֥ן עָשׂ֖וּ בְּנ֥וֹת צְלָפְחָֽד׃ Greek (Septuagint / Brenton) Ὃν τρόπον συνέταξε Κύριος Μωυσῇ, οὕτως ἐποίησαν θυγατράσι Σαλπαάδ. ↩ Numbers 36:11“for Mahlah, Tirzah, Hoglah, Milcah, and Noah, the daughters of Zelophehad, were married to their father’s brothers’ sons.” Hebrew (Masoretic / WLC) וַתִּהְיֶ֜ינָה מַחְלָ֣ה תִרְצָ֗ה וְחָגְלָ֧ה וּמִלְכָּ֛ה וְנֹעָ֖ה בְּנ֣וֹת צְלָפְחָ֑ד לִבְנֵ֥י דֹדֵיהֶ֖ן לְנָשִֽׁים׃ Greek (Septuagint / Brenton) Καὶ ἐγένοντο Θερσὰ καὶ Ἐγλὰ καὶ Μελχὰ καὶ Νούα καὶ Μαλαὰ θυγατέρες Σαλπαὰδ, τοῖς ἀνεψιοῖς αὐτῶν, ↩ Numbers 36:12“They were married into the families of the sons of Manasseh the son of Joseph. Their inheritance remained in the tribe of the family of their father.” Hebrew (Masoretic / WLC) מִֽמִּשְׁפְּחֹ֛ת בְּנֵֽי־מְנַשֶּׁ֥ה בֶן־יוֹסֵ֖ף הָי֣וּ לְנָשִׁ֑ים וַתְּהִי֙ נַחֲלָתָ֔ן עַל־מַטֵּ֖ה מִשְׁפַּ֥חַת אֲבִיהֶֽן׃ Greek (Septuagint / Brenton) ἐκ τοῦ δήμου τοῦ Μανασσῆ υἱῶν Ἰωσὴφ ἐγενήθησαν γυναῖκες· καὶ ἐγενήθη ἡ κληρονομία αὐτῶν ἐπὶ τὴν φυλὴν δήμου τοῦ πατρὸς αὐτῶν. ↩ Numbers 36:13“These are the commandments and the ordinances which Yahweh commanded by Moses to the children of Israel in the plains of Moab by the Jordan at Jericho.” Hebrew (Masoretic / WLC) אֵ֣לֶּה הַמִּצְוֺ֞ת וְהַמִּשְׁפָּטִ֗ים אֲשֶׁ֨ר צִוָּ֧ה יְהוָ֛ה בְּיַד־מֹשֶׁ֖ה אֶל־בְּנֵ֣י יִשְׂרָאֵ֑ל בְּעַֽרְבֹ֣ת מוֹאָ֔ב עַ֖ל יַרְדֵּ֥ן יְרֵחֽוֹ׃ Greek (Septuagint / Brenton) Αὗται αἱ ἐντολαὶ καὶ τὰ δικαιώματα καὶ τὰ κρίματα, ἃ ἐνετείλατο Κύριος ἐν χειρὶ Μωυσῆ ἐπὶ δυσμῶν Μωὰβ ἐπὶ τοῦ Ἰορδάνου κατὰ Ἰεριχώ. ↩”

Hebrew (Masoretic / WLC)

וֶֽהֱשִֽׁיבְךָ֨ יְהוָ֥ה ׀ מִצְרַיִם֮ בָּאֳנִיּוֹת֒ בַּדֶּ֙רֶךְ֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר אָמַ֣רְתִּֽי לְךָ֔ לֹא־תֹסִ֥יף ע֖וֹד לִרְאֹתָ֑הּ וְהִתְמַכַּרְתֶּ֨ם שָׁ֧ם לְאֹיְבֶ֛יךָ לַעֲבָדִ֥ים וְלִשְׁפָח֖וֹת וְאֵ֥ין קֹנֶֽה׃

Greek (Septuagint / Brenton)

Καὶ ἀποστρέψει σε Κύριος εἰς Αἴγυπτον ἐν πλοίοις, ἐν τῇ ὁδῷ ἡ· εἶπα, οὐ προσθήσῃ ἔτι ἰδεῖν αὐτήν· καὶ πραθήσεσθε ἐκεῖ τοῖς ἐχθροῖς ὑμῶν εἰς παῖδας καὶ παιδίσκας, καὶ οὐκ ἔσται ὁ κτώμενος.
